common_name: Garden's Guardian Stewartia (Dwarf Compact Chinese Stewartia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade, and avoid disturbing the root zone once established.

directions: This is a compact seedling selection of Chinese stewartia found by plantsman Crispin Silva roughly a decade ago, chosen for staying dense, bushy, and columnar rather than growing into the larger upright tree typical of the species. It bears the same white, camellia-like summer flowers as straight Stewartia sinensis, followed by fall foliage that turns a brilliant red-orange. Because the original plant stayed under 2 feet wide after many years, it suits small gardens where a full-size stewartia would not fit. Give it the same care as the species: consistent moisture, acidic humus-rich soil, and shelter from hot afternoon sun.

common_name: Pillar Bella Stewartia (Narrow Columnar Japanese Stewartia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade where its narrow footprint allows siting close to walkways or small borders.

directions: Selected by plantsman Crispin Silva, this cultivar grows as a strikingly narrow, upright column rather than the broader pyramidal form typical of Japanese stewartia, with a 15-year-old reference plant reaching about 12 feet tall but only 3 feet wide. Its white, cupped summer flowers are comparable in size to those of the similarly narrow cultivar 'Ballet', but held on a much slimmer tree. That tight columnar habit makes it useful as a vertical accent in gardens too small for a standard stewartia. Grow it as you would the species, in moist, acidic, well-drained soil with partial shade and protection from drying wind.

common_name: Grape Expectations Magnolia (Grape Bubblegum-Scented Kobus Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, sheltered from late frost since this kobus-type magnolia blooms on bare wood.

directions: A kobus-type magnolia named for its unusual scent, Grape Expectations opens modest 3 to 4 inch white-tepaled flowers on bare branches in early spring, with a fragrance the nursery describes as distinctly like grape bubble gum rather than the citrusy or spicy notes typical of most magnolias. It grows vigorously, in keeping with the kobus lineage behind many cold-hardy hybrid magnolias. Site it in full sun on moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and choose a spot sheltered from hard spring frosts that could damage the early flowers. It makes a worthwhile specimen tree for gardeners who want a conversation-starting fragrance alongside typical spring magnolia bloom.

common_name: Lorie's Fire Magnolia (Yellow and Red Bicolor Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; this vigorous hybrid benefits from room to grow out its spreading branches.

directions: Bred by hybridizer Ray Tessmer as a seedling selection from Phil Savage's yellow-flowered 'Golden Sun', Lorie's Fire produces bicolor blooms with yellow tepals flushed red toward the base, a warmer effect than the purely yellow magnolias common in the Savage breeding line. The tree grows vigorously, quickly building a substantial branch structure once established. Plant it in full sun on moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil, and give it enough space for a full-size flowering magnolia, since vigorous hybrids like this one size up faster than many named cultivars. It suits gardeners wanting an unusual bicolor bloom beyond the standard pink, white, or solid-yellow magnolia palette.

common_name: Angel Eyes Oyama Magnolia (Upright Selection with Showy Stamens)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in partial shade sheltered from wind, since the nodding flowers and upright branching are easily damaged by exposure.

directions: Selected out of a batch of Magnolia sieboldii seedlings, Angel Eyes stands out for growing distinctly more upright and vertical than the typically broad, spreading species, and for carrying larger, showier stamens in the center of each flower. Like the species, its fragrant white cup-shaped flowers nod downward below the foliage in late spring and early summer, best appreciated from below or on a slope. The more vertical habit makes it a better fit than species-type Oyama magnolia for narrower garden spaces. Grow it in partial shade with moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and shelter from strong wind, as for other Magnolia sieboldii.

common_name: Winter Glow Climbing Hydrangea (Evergreen Climbing Hydrangea with Glossy Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring against a sturdy wall, fence, or tree trunk in partial shade, giving the clinging stems a surface they can attach to right away.

directions: Unlike the deciduous climbing hydrangea most gardeners know, this selection keeps glossy green leaves through the winter, giving the vine year-round presence on a wall or trunk rather than bare stems in the off season. It produces the familiar white lacecap flower clusters in early summer, typical of climbing hydrangea types. As a woody climber it needs a sturdy support to cling to and takes time to establish before it climbs vigorously. Grow it in partial shade with consistently moist, well-drained soil, and expect it to be somewhat less cold-hardy than deciduous climbing hydrangea given its evergreen foliage.

common_name: Purple Eye Yulan Magnolia (Ivory Magnolia with Purple-Striped Base)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, allowing extra lateral room for its more spreading-than-usual habit.

directions: This yulan magnolia selection carries ivory-white tepals marked with a distinct purple stripe at the base of each petal, a color detail absent from plain Magnolia denudata. Gossler Farms also notes that it grows with a more horizontally spreading habit than the species type, rather than the more upright form typical of yulan magnolia. Like other denudata forms, it blooms on bare branches in early spring before the leaves emerge, so choose a site sheltered from hard late frosts. Grow it in full sun on moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and allow it the wider lateral space its spreading habit calls for.

common_name: Marjory Gossler Magnolia (Large Pink-Blush Hybrid Named for the Nursery's Founder)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, choosing a site with room for a large shade tree over time.

directions: A cross between Magnolia sargentiana 'Blood Moon' and Magnolia denudata, bred jointly by hybridizer Phil Savage and Gossler Farms Nursery, this cultivar was named in honor of Marj Gossler of the nursery's founding family. Its flowers open with a soft pink blush that fades quickly to white, a transitional color effect distinct from magnolias that hold pink through the whole bloom. Gossler Farms describes it as developing into a large 40-foot tree and notes it has proven very cold hardy, tolerating climates as harsh as Detroit's. Give it full sun, moist fertile well-drained soil, and plenty of room to grow into its eventual size as a substantial specimen tree.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in fall or spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, protected from hot afternoon sun that can stress the foliage.

directions: Found by plantsman Guy Meacham, this Japanese stewartia selection is distinguished mainly by a distinctive silvery overcast on its foliage, setting it apart visually from the plain dark green leaves of the species. In all other respects, including its white, camellia-like summer flowers, it matches standard Stewartia pseudocamellia, and it should also share the species' exfoliating multicolored bark and strong fall color. Use it exactly as you would other Japanese stewartia: moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil, partial shade, and protection from hot, dry exposure, with minimal root disturbance once planted.
